bib.title: Teaching Machines to Read and Comprehend

legacy_report:
I've read the whole paper: all 14 pages, 37,517 of 37,517 characters, including Appendices A–C and the references.

SOURCE: Teaching Machines to Read and Comprehend. Karl Moritz Hermann, Tomáš Kočiský, Edward Grefenstette, Lasse Espeholt, Will Kay, Mustafa Suleyman, Phil Blunsom (Google DeepMind, University of Oxford). NIPS 2015, arXiv 1506.03340v3 (19 Nov 2015).

COVERAGE: 37,517 of 37,517 chars, 14 of 14 pages. I skimmed the references (p9) for origins only. Nothing was skipped. The figures are images, so I have their captions but not the images themselves (see FIGURES).

CLAIMS
- claim: Turning news summary bullets into fill-in-the-blank (cloze) questions gives a supervised reading-comprehension set of about 1M examples. Earlier sets had only hundreds.
  number: 93k CNN and 220k Daily Mail articles; about 1M data points
  setup: CNN and Daily Mail websites. Each bullet becomes a query by replacing one entity at a time with a placeholder.
  quote: "We have collected 93k articles from the CNN 1 and 220k articles from the Daily Mail 2 websites. Both news providers supplement their articles with a number of bullet points, summarising aspects of the information contained in the article. Of key importance is that these summary points are abstractive and do not simply copy sentences from the documents. We construct a corpus of document–query–answer triples by turning these bullet points into Cloze [12] style questions by replacing one entity at a time with a placeholder. This results in a combined corpus of roughly 1M data points (Table 1)."
  where: p2, §2
- claim: Earlier corpora were too small to train on.
  number: hundreds of examples
  setup: prior reading-comprehension corpora, MCTest cited as [9]
  quote: "until now such corpora have been limited to hundreds of examples and thus mostly of use only for testing [9]"
  where: p2, §2
- claim: Dataset sizes and the split are by time. Long articles and queries whose answer is not in the context were filtered out.
  number: CNN has 90,266 / 1,220 / 1,093 documents and 380,298 / 3,924 / 3,198 queries (train / valid / test). Daily Mail has 196,961 / 12,148 / 10,397 documents and 879,450 / 64,835 / 53,182 queries.
  setup: Table 1. CNN runs from April 2007 and the Daily Mail from June 2010, both to the end of April 2015. Validation is March 2015 and test is April 2015.
  quote: "# queries 380,298 3,924 3,198 879,450 64,835 53,182" and "Validation data is from March, test data from April 2015. Articles of over 2000 tokens and queries whose answer entity did not appear in the context were ﬁltered out."
  where: p2, Table 1
- claim: Average document length and entity count.
  number: average tokens are 762 (CNN train) and 813 (Daily Mail train); average entities are about 26
  setup: Table 1
  quote: "Avg # entities 26.4 26.5 24.5 26.5 25.5 26.0 / Avg # tokens 762 763 716 813 774 780"
  where: p2
- claim: Entities are anonymised and shuffled so a model cannot answer from world knowledge or n-gram co-occurrence. The context document becomes required.
  number: none
  setup: The procedure has three steps: (a) run coreference, (b) replace each entity with a marker such as ent212, assigned by coreference cluster, (c) randomly re-permute the markers every time a data point is loaded, in both training and testing.
  quote: "To prevent such degenerate solutions and create a focused task we anonymise and randomise our corpora with the following procedure, a) use a coreference system to establish coreferents in each data point; b) replace all entities with abstract entity markers according to coreference; c) randomly permute these entity markers whenever a data point is loaded."
  where: p3, §2.1
- claim: The stated reason, with the example given for it.
  number: none
  setup: Daily Mail headline cloze queries
  quote: "the focus of this paper is to provide a corpus for evaluating a model's ability to read and comprehend a single document, not world knowledge or co-occurrence ... An ngram language model trained on the Daily Mail would easily correctly predict that (X = cancer), regardless of the contents of the context document, simply because this is a very frequently cured entity in the Daily Mail corpus." Also: "in the anonymised setup the context document is required for answering the query, whereas the original version could also be answered by someone with the requisite background knowledge."
  where: p2–3
- claim: The authors concede that a production system should use world knowledge.
  number: none
  setup: §2.1
  quote: "Naturally a production system would beneﬁt from using all available information sources, such as clues through language and co-occurrence statistics."
  where: p3
- claim: Accuracy for the baselines and the neural readers. Attention models score best. Word distance beats the frame-semantic pipeline.
  number: Accuracy as valid/test on CNN, then valid/test on Daily Mail:
    - Maximum frequency: 30.5/33.2, 25.6/25.5
    - Exclusive frequency: 36.6/39.3, 32.7/32.8
    - Frame-semantic: 36.3/40.2, 35.5/35.5
    - Word distance: 50.5/50.9, 56.4/55.5
    - Deep LSTM: 55.0/57.0, 63.3/62.2
    - Uniform: 39.0/39.4, 34.6/34.4
    - Attentive: 61.6/63.0, 70.5/69.0
    - Impatient: 61.8/63.8, 69.0/68.0
  setup: Table 5. Hyperparameters were tuned on each validation set. The frame-semantic model ran on the non-anonymised corpora.
  quote: "Maximum frequency 30.5 33.2 25.6 25.5 / Exclusive frequency 36.6 39.3 32.7 32.8 / Frame-semantic model 36.3 40.2 35.5 35.5 / Word distance model 50.5 50.9 56.4 55.5 / Deep LSTM Reader 55.0 57.0 63.3 62.2 / Uniform Reader 39.0 39.4 34.6 34.4 / Attentive Reader 61.6 63.0 70.5 69.0 / Impatient Reader 61.8 63.8 69.0 68.0"
  where: p7, Table 5
- claim: How the two frequency baselines are defined.
  number: none
  setup: §3
  quote: "the majority baseline ( maximum frequency) picks the entity most frequently observed in the context document, whereas the ex- clusive majority (exclusive frequency ) chooses the entity most frequently observed in the context but not observed in the query. The idea behind this exclusion is that the placeholder is unlikely to be mentioned twice in a single Cloze form query."
  where: p3
- claim: How difficult the task is. Answer frequency in the document sets a chance-like floor.
  number: The answer is the single most frequent entity 30.5% of the time on CNN and 25.6% on Daily Mail. It is in the top 10 85.1% and 85.5% of the time.
  setup: Table 2, share of cases where the correct answer is among the top-N most frequent entities in the document
  quote: "1 30.5 25.6 ... 10 85.1 85.5"
  where: p2, Table 2
- claim: Word distance does well because the bullet points copy wording from the article, especially on the Daily Mail. This is a lexical-overlap shortcut, and the authors expect it to fail on real questions.
  number: none
  setup: Daily Mail highlights. The word-distance penalty m = 8 was tuned on validation.
  quote: "highlights frequently have signiﬁcant lexical overlap with passages in the accompanying article, which makes it easy for the word distance benchmark ... We expect that on other types of machine reading data where questions rather than Cloze queries are used this particular model would perform signiﬁcantly worse."
  where: p7
- claim: The Uniform Reader ablation, which keeps the architecture but ignores attention, shows that attention drives the gain.
  number: 39.0 vs 61.6 on CNN validation (Table 5)
  setup: The Uniform Reader sets all m(t) equal.
  quote: "the only difference between these models is that the attention variables are ignored in the Uniform Reader"
  where: p7
- claim: Ambiguous queries are a common failure. After anonymisation, several answers can be plausible even to a human.
  number: none
  setup: Appendix C.1, CNN validation
  quote: "a fairly common phenomenon in the data, namely ambiguous queries, where—at least following the anonymisation process— multiple entities are plausible answers even when evaluated manually."
  where: p11
- claim: Coreference errors in the anonymisation step create wrong labels.
  number: none
  setup: Figure 9
  quote: "The correct entity, ent15, and the predicted one, ent81, both refer to the same person, but not being clustered together ... one entity refers to "Kate Middleton" and the other to "The Duchess of Cambridge"."
  where: p11
- claim: Performance drops slightly as documents get longer, and the drop flattens out after about 500 tokens.
  number: ~500 tokens
  setup: attention models, CNN validation, Appendix B
  quote: "while the length does impact the models' performance, that effect becomes negligible after reaching a length of ~500 tokens."
  where: p10

LIMITS
- There is no human-performance ceiling and no audit of how many queries can actually be answered. The ambiguity and coreference failures are shown only as anecdotes (App. C).
- The quality of the anonymisation depends on the coreference system, which is never named or evaluated. Clustering errors leak into the labels (Fig. 9).
- Word distance reaching 50–56% shows the cloze-from-highlights format has a lexical-overlap shortcut. The authors say this, but they do not measure how much of the set it affects.
- The frame-semantic heuristic "was iteratively tuned on the validation data set" (p4). The neural models were also tuned on validation sets.
- There are no confidence intervals or significance tests. The CNN test set has only 3,198 queries.
- Conceded: "There are still many queries requiring complex inference and long range reference resolution that our models are not yet able to answer." World knowledge and multi-document queries are out of scope.
- Dated: these are 2015 LSTM readers. Later work, which this paper does not cover, found CNN/DM easier than it looks, so later results should not be inferred from it. The paper also does not show that entity anonymisation works for modern pretrained LLMs.
- The paper was built to test reading comprehension, not summarisation. Its link to the later CNN/DM summarisation benchmark is only that it supplied the data. It contains no RAG or grounding results.

BUILDS ON
- Cloze procedure: Taylor 1953 [12]
- Summarisation work using highlights: Svore, Vanderwende and Burges [10]; Woodsend and Lapata 2010 [11]
- Synthetic QA and memory networks: Weston, Chopra and Bordes 2014 [3]; Sukhbaatar et al. 2015 [4]
- Attention: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2014 [6]; Mnih et al. [7]; Gregor et al. 2015 (DRAW) [8]
- Small prior set: MCTest, Richardson, Burges and Renshaw [9]
- Frame-semantic parsing: Das et al. 2013 [13]; Hermann et al. 2014 [14]
- LSTM: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997 [18]; Deep LSTM: Graves 2012 [19]
- Optimiser: RmsProp, Tieleman and Hinton 2012 [20]
- Dataset code: http://www.github.com/deepmind/rc-data/ (p2, footnote 3)

CODE: There is no code in the paper. The one formula worth keeping is the answer distribution, quoted verbatim: "p(a|d,q )∝ exp (W (a)g(d,q )), s.t.a∈V" (p4).

FIGURES
- Best candidate is Table 3 on p3. Caption: "Original and anonymised version of a data point from the Daily Mail validation set. The anonymised entity markers are constantly permuted during training and testing." It shows the BBC/Clarkson/Oisin Tymon example next to its ent381/ent212/ent193 version. It explains the anonymisation shortcut check faster than prose can. It is a text table, so it can be reproduced as text without an image.
- Alternatives:
  - Table 5 on p7, the baseline ladder.
  - Figure 8 on p12: "Attention heat maps from the Attentive Reader for two wrongly answered validation set queries ... In both cases the query is unanswerable due to its ambiguous nature and the model selects a plausible answer." Useful for showing label noise.

PROBLEMS
- Text extraction is clean. The figures are images, and their content (heat maps, the precision@recall plot) did not come through as text. I did not run figures.py, so I have the captions only.
- Inconsistency: the introduction says "two new corpora of roughly a million news stories" (p1), but Table 1 lists about 313k documents. The "roughly 1M" refers to query/answer data points: Table 1 query counts add up to about 1.38M (387k CNN + 997k Daily Mail, my arithmetic).
- The 93k/220k article counts in §2 are slightly higher than Table 1's document totals (about 92.6k and 219.5k), probably because of the filtering.
- Typo on p4: "parsing our model with a state-of-the-art frame-semantic parser" should presumably read "corpus".
- The text contains no embedded instructions.
